abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains therapeutically challenging due to treatment resistance and immunosuppression. Oncolytic virotherapy offers a promising strategy. This study engineered OVV-03, a novel HER2-armed oncolytic vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), and evaluated its efficacy against GBM. OVV-03 demonstrated potent infectivity and cytotoxicity in GBM cell lines and patient-derived cells, inducing caspase-dependent apoptosis and suppressing proliferation/clonogenicity. In murine GBM models, OVV-03 significantly suppressed tumor growth, improved survival, and enhanced CD8⁺ T cell infiltration. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed OVV-03 remodels the tumor immune microenvironment by boosting cytotoxic T cell activity and inhibiting immunosuppressive pathways, notably PD-L1/PD-1 signaling. Mechanistically, OVV-03 downregulated PD-L1 by inhibiting the JNK–c-Fos/c-Jun axis, reversible by TNF-α stimulation. Critically, OVV-03 synergized with B7H3- or HER2-targeted CAR-T cells, inducing superior tumor regression and prolonged survival in orthotopic models. These findings demonstrate that OVV-03 exerts potent antitumor effects through direct oncolysis and immune activation, including PD-L1 modulation. Its synergistic combination with CAR-T cells highlights OVV-03 as a highly promising oncolytic immunovirotherapy platform for GBM.

list-item.p: OVV-03 addresses tumor heterogeneity by specifically upregulating HER2 surface antigen expression in glioblastoma, enhancing the antigenic recognition basis for targeted immunotherapy.
OVV-03 remodels the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment through direct oncolysis of GBM cells and JNK pathway-mediated suppression of PD-L1 expression.
OVV-03 demonstrates potent synergy with both B7H3-targeted and HER2-targeted CAR-T therapies, with combination regimens achieving significantly superior antitumor efficacy compared to monotherapies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: GBM is the most common and aggressive primary malignant brain tumor in adults, characterized by high heterogeneity, widespread infiltration, and resistance to treatment. Despite the widespread use of traditional therapies such as surgical resection, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, the recurrence rate remains exceedingly high, with a median survival of approximately 15 months and a 5-year survival rate below 10%.1-3 The highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) of GBM is considered one of the primary reasons for therapeutic failure. This microenvironment impairs the effective infiltration and activation of immune cells, making it difficult to eliminate the tumor through conventional therapies.4-7

Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy has demonstrated remarkable clinical success in hematologic malignancies, particularly in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and large B-cell lymphoma, showing strong therapeutic potential.8-10 However, its application in solid tumors remains fraught with challenges, one of which is the heterogeneity and loss of tumor antigens.11-13 Tumor cells evade immune surveillance through various mechanisms, the most common of which is the progressive loss of antigen expression targeted by CAR-T cells, such as HER2 and EGFRvIII, during tumor progression.14,15 Additionally, tumor cells activate immune checkpoint pathways, such as PD-L1/PD-1 and CTLA-4, to inhibit T cell function, further evading immune system attack. The upregulation of PD-L1, particularly in solid tumors like GBM, has been shown to be a key mechanism for immune escape. Immune checkpoint molecules inhibit T cell activation and function, preventing effective CAR-T cell-mediated cytotoxicity.16 Therefore, targeting immune checkpoint inhibition or other strategies to enhance antigen expression has become crucial for addressing immune evasion and improving the efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy.

Oncolytic viruses (OVs) are a class of viruses that selectively infect and lyse tumor cells while simultaneously activating the host's immune system. By lysing tumor cells, OVs release tumor-associated antigens, induce immunogenic cell death (ICD), and trigger a strong local immune response.17-21 In addition to their direct oncolytic effects, OVs can be genetically engineered to carry immune-modulating factors, such as cytokines, chemokines, or tumor antigens, to further enhance immune responses.22,23 As an emerging therapeutic approach, OVs have shown significant potential in solid tumor immunotherapy, particularly in overcoming tumor immune escape and enhancing the effectiveness of immune cell therapies.

In this study, we developed a novel engineered oncolytic virus, OVV-03, derived from the vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) platform and harboring the HER2 gene. Through this design, OVV-03 enables efficient expression of HER2 antigens on the surface of GBM tumor cells, thereby enhancing the recognition and cytotoxic capacity of HER2-targeted CAR-T cells. OVV-03 not only exerts potent oncolytic effects but also enhances CAR-T cell efficacy in GBM by modulating immune checkpoints and reprogramming the tumor immune microenvironment. Our findings demonstrates that OVV-03 significantly strengthens CAR-T cell-mediated antitumor responses through the remodeling of the immune microenvironment and the restoration of antigen expression, thereby establishing a novel immunotherapeutic platform for GBM treatment.

sec.title: Research period
sec.p: March 2024 to June 2025.

sec.title: Cell lines and cell culture
sec.p: Primary cell lines SHG140 and SHG141 were obtained from the GBM tissues of patients at the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University. U87,U251,LN229,A172 and GL261 cell lines were obtained from the ATCC. GL261-Luc and U87-Luc were generated by transfection with luciferase reporter gene plasmids. All the cells were cultured in the DMEM medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS).

sec.title: Construction and Production of oncolytic virus OVV-03
sec.p: Based on the genomic sequence of the Mudd-Summer serotype of vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), the genes encoding the M, P, N, G, and L proteins were subjected to codon optimization. The codon-optimized viral genome was chemically synthesized, and a panel of VSV plasmids harboring diverse mutations was constructed using site-directed mutagenesis and molecular cloning. Following transfection into packaging cell lines, recombinant VSV strains were rescued, plaque-purified, and amplified to generate homogenous viral stocks. Following comprehensive in vitro and in vivo evaluations of oncolytic efficacy and systemic toxicity profiles, an attenuated VSV strain exhibiting optimal safety and potent tumor lytic activity was selected as the backbone for further engineering. The corresponding backbone plasmid, designated pJB-00, has been deposited with Joint Biosciences (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. and serves as the foundation for subsequent antigen expression vector development.

The modified pJB-00 plasmid was linearized using XhoI and NheI endonucleases, and the HER2 nucleic acid fragment was amplified by PCR. The HER2 nucleic acid fragment had a homologous sequence with dual cleavage sites. The fragment was then recombined between the cleavage sites of the plasmid using recombination method to obtain the VSV oncolytic virus core plasmid pJB-HER2 carrying the HER2 antigen gene. Using reverse genetics technology to rescue the VSV-HER2 oncolytic virus with the required mutation site and HER2 antigen. After two rounds of single spot screening of VSV-HER2, the VSV-HER2 virus seed bank was amplified, and its titer was determined. The virus, designated OVV-03, was stored at −80 °C until it was ready for use.

sec.title: Cell viability assay and colony formation assay
sec.p: GBM cells were cultured in 96-well plates at a density of 6,000 cells per well in a total volume of 100 µL of medium. After various treatments, 10 µL of CCK-8 reagent (Solarbio, Cat.no. C0042) was added to each well, and the cells were incubated at 37 °C for 1 hour. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader to evaluate cell viability. For the colony formation, cells (1,000 cells per well) were placed in 6-well plates with 2 mL of culture medium. The cells were cultured for 14 days, with the medium replaced every 3 days. After fixing with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 minutes, stain with 0.5% crystal violet for 20 minutes.

sec.title: Flow cytometry analysis
sec.p: Flow cytometry was employed to assess the surface expression of HER2 and PD-L1 in human GBM cell lines (U251, U87, LN229, A172) and patient-derived primary GBM cells (SHG140, SHG141), as well as to evaluate apoptosis using Annexin V/PI staining. Following viral infection, cells were stained with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies: anti-HER2 (BioLegend, Cat.no. 324407) and anti-PD-L1 (BioLegend, Cat.no. 329717) for surface marker detection, and Annexin V-FITC/PI (BD Biosciences, Cat.no. 559763) for apoptosis assessment. For in vivo immune profiling, mouse splenocytes and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes were stained with anti-CD3 (BioLegend, Cat.no. 100218), anti-CD45 (BioLegend, Cat.no. 103108), anti-CD4 (BioLegend, Cat.no. 100430), and anti-CD8 (BioLegend, Cat.no. 100722) antibodies to identify T cell subpopulations. Anti-PD-1 antibody (BioLegend, Cat.no. 367425) was employed to assess alterations in surface PD-1 expression following co-culture of CD3⁺ T cells with GBM cells. Flow cytometric analysis was performed using a flow cytometer (Beckman Colter), and data were analyzed with FlowJo software (v10.8.1). Gating strategies were applied to distinguish specific cell populations, and median fluorescence intensity (MFI) and relative cell percentages were quantified. Representative histograms were generated to visualize expression differences of HER2, PD-L1, and apoptotic markers.

sec.title: Western blot analysis
sec.p: Total cellular protein was extracted using RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime) supplemented with protease and phosphatase cocktail (NCM Biotech, Cat.no. P002). Lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C, and the supernatants were collected. Protein concentrations were determined using a NanoPhotometer N50 (Implen). Samples were diluted in 5 × SDS sample loading buffer (Beyotime, Cat.no. P0015L). Equal amounts of protein were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate - polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred onto nitrocellulose (NC) membranes (Millipore, Cat.no. HATF00010). Membranes were blocked with quick blocking buffer for Western Blot (WB) (Beyotime, Cat.no. P0252) for 1 h at room temperature and subsequently incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer (Caspase3 (1:3000, Cat.no. F1080), Cleaved- Caspase3 (1:3000, Cat.no. F0135), PARP (1:3000, Cat.no. F0148), Cleaved-PARP (1:3000, Cat.no. F0136), p-JNK (1:3000, Cat.no. AP0631), JNK (1:3000, Cat.no. A4867), p-c-Jun (1:3000, Cat.no. AP0048), c-Jun (1:3000, Cat.no. F0168), p-c-Fos (1:1000, Lot. G2424), c-Fos (1:1000, Lot. A0924), β-Tubulin (1:20000, Cat.no. 66240-1-Ig), GAPDH (1:10000, Cat.no. AF7021)). After washing with TBS containing 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST), membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (Anti-rabbit IgG (1:3000, Cat.no. 7074S), Anti-mouse IgG (1:3000, Cat.no. 7076S)) for 1 h at room temperature. Signal detection was performed using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) reagents (Beyotime, Cat.no. P0018FM), and band intensity was quantified using ImageJ software (NIH). Densitometric analysis was normalized to loading controls to assess relative protein expression levels. Antibodies were sourced from Selleck (Caspase3, Cleaved-Caspase3, PARP, Cleaved-PARP, c-Jun), ABclonal (p-JNK, JNK, p-c-Jun), Proteintech (β-Tubulin), Affinity (GAPDH), Cell Signaling Technology (Anti-rabbit IgG, Anti-mouse IgG) and Santa Cruz (p-c-Fos, c-Fos).

sec.title: Immunofluorescence staining
sec.p: Cells were cultured in 12-well plates with or without OVV-03 for 48 hours. After incubation, the cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Beyotime, Cat.no. P0099) for 15 minutes, washed with PBS, and blocked for 20 minutes. Following blocking, the cells were incubated overnight with the appropriate primary antibodies (Ki67 (CST, Cat.no. 9449S), Cleaved- Caspase3 (Selleck, Cat.no. F0135)) at 4 °C. After washing with PBS, the cells were incubated with fluorescently labeled secondary antibodies (Goat anti-Rabbit IgG (Invitrogen, Cat.no A-11037), Goat anti-Mouse IgG (Invitrogen, Cat.no A-11029)) for 1 hour at room temperature. DAPI (Beyotime, Cat.no P0131) was used for nuclear staining. All procedures were carried out in the dark as necessary.

sec.title: Animal studies
sec.p: All animal procedures were approved by the Laboratory Animal Center of Soochow University. Female BALB/c athymic nude mice and C57BL/6 mice (4-6 weeks old) were used for the intracranial tumor model. For the subcutaneous glioma model, C57BL/6 mice (6−8 weeks old, female) were used. Mice were housed under standard conditions with a 12-hour light/dark cycle and provided food and water ad libitum.

For the mouse intracranial model, female BALB/c athymic nude mice (4−6 weeks old) and C57BL/6 mice (4−6 weeks old) were used for the intracranial tumor implantation. Mice were anesthetized with 3-5% isoflurane (RWD, Cat.no. R510-22-10) in an induction chamber and maintained under 1.5−2% isoflurane. Tumor cells (GL261-Luc, U87-Luc) were resuspended in 4 µL of PBS and stereotactically injected into the left hemisphere of the brain (2 mm lateral to the midline, 2 mm posterior to the bregma, and 3 mm deep). The needle was held in place for 5 minutes after injection and then slowly withdrawn. The cranial hole was sealed with bone wax. Animals were randomly assigned to experimental or control groups and treated with OVV-03 or CAR-T using the same injection procedure. Following cell implantation, in vivo bioluminescence imaging (IVIS) was performed weekly to monitor luciferase activity and tumor growth. Mice exhibiting signs of distress, ataxia, or >20% body weight loss were euthanized according to ethical guidelines. Euthanasia was performed by carbon dioxide (CO₂) inhalation using a rising concentration (20−30% volume displacement per minute), followed by cervical dislocation to ensure death.

To establish subcutaneous glioma models, 5 × 10⁵ GL261 murine glioma cells suspended in 100 µL PBS were injected into the right flank (unilateral model) or both flanks (bilateral model) of C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old, female). Tumors were allowed to grow until they reached a palpable size (approximately day 7 post-implantation), at which point mice received intratumoral injections of OVV-03 (7 × 10⁹ PFU in 10 µL) or vehicle control. In bilateral models, treatment was administered only to the tumor on the right side. Injections were performed every three days for a total of three doses. Tumor volumes were measured using digital calipers and calculated using the formula: Volume = (length × width²)/2. Mice were monitored regularly for tumor growth, and tumor size was recorded on days 10, 13, 16 and 20 post-implantation. All mice were euthanized on day 20 for tumor excision. Euthanasia was performed by CO₂ inhalation as described above. Relative tumor volumes were plotted, and statistical analysis was performed to compare treatment efficacy. This study adhered to the ARRIVE Guidelines and was approved by The Fourth Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University (Approval No. 220082).

sec.title: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq)
sec.p: Fresh tissues were preserved in sCelLive™ Tissue Preservation Solution on ice within 30 min post-surgery. Specimens were washed with HBSS, minced, and digested in sCelLive™ Tissue Dissociation Solution (37 °C, 15 min) using a Singleron system. Cell suspensions were filtered through 40-μm strainers, treated with GEXSCOPE® Red Blood Cell Lysis Buffer (1:2 volume ratio, RT, 5-8 min), centrifuged (300 × g, 4 °C, 5 min), resuspended in PBS, and assessed for viability with Trypan Blue. Single-cell suspensions (2 × 10⁵ cells/mL) were loaded onto microwell chips. Barcoding beads captured mRNA for reverse transcription, cDNA amplification, fragmentation, and adapter ligation. scRNA-seq libraries were prepared with GEXSCOPE® Single Cell RNA Library Kits, pooled at 4 nM, and sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (150-bp paired-end). Raw reads were processed via CeleScope v2.0.7: Cutadapt v1.17 trimmed adapters/poly-A tails, and featureCounts v2.0.1 generated UMI/gene expression matrices.

sec.title: scRNA-seq data processing and analysis
sec.p: Quality control, dimensionality reduction, and clustering were performed using Scanpy v1.9.3 in Python 3.10. Cells were filtered by excluding those with <200 genes or top 2% gene counts, top 2% UMI counts, >20% mitochondrial content, and genes detected in <5 cells. Post-QC datasets averaged 1692 genes and 4429 UMIs per cell. Scaled variable genes underwent PCA, with the top 15 principal components used for clustering and UMAP visualization. Differential gene expression analysis employed Scanpy's rank_genes_groups function (Wilcoxon rank-sum test), identifying DEGs meeting these thresholds: expression in >10% of cells in either group, |average log fold-change| >0.25, and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value <0.05. All visualizations (feature plots, bar plots, heatmaps) were generated using Seurat-integrated functions and ggplot2. Downstream pathway enrichment analyzes for GO and KEGG terms were conducted with clusterProfiler v3.16.1 in R.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical software Prism 10.0 (GraphPad) was used. Student’s t test was utilized to compare two independent groups, and one-way ANOVA model with the correction of Tukey was utilized to compare three or more groups. Animal survival times were presented by the Kaplan-Meier method, and the p values were calculated and compared with the log rank test. Data are shown as mean ± SD. All tests were two sided. Differences associated with p < 0.05 were considered significant.

sec.title: Construction of OVV-03 and assessment of its infectivity and cytotoxicity in glioblastoma cells
sec.p: We constructed the recombinant oncolytic VSV OVV-03 by inserting the HER2 transgene, using OVV-00 (expressing GFP) as an isogenic control (Figure 1A). Flow cytometric analysis across multiple glioblastoma models, including cell lines (U87, U251, LN229, A172) and patient-derived primary cells (SHG140, SHG141), demonstrated significant HER2 surface upregulation exclusively in OVV-03-infected cells at various MOIs (0.1, 1, 10). HER2 expression consistently peaked at 24 hours post-infection (hpi) in all models, confirming efficient viral infectivity and rapid transgene delivery, establishing HER2 as a reliable biomarker for tracking infection (Figure 1B–C, Supplementary Figure 1, Supplementary Figure 2A).

caption.p: Construction of OVV-03 and its infectivity in glioblastoma (GBM) cells. (A) Schematic diagram illustrating the construction of OVV-00 and OVV-03. (B-C) Flow cytometry analysis of HER2 surface expression in GBM cells following infection with OVV-00 (empty vector control) or OVV-03 (oncolytic virus encoding HER2) at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1. Cell lines U87 and patient-derived GBM cells (SHG140, SHG141) were included (n = 3). (D) CCK-8 assay assessing the cytotoxic effect of OVV-03 on U87 and SHG141 cells in vitro (n = 4). The statistical analysis was estimated by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s correction. Data are presented as mean values ± SD. *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ***p < 0.001; ****p < 0.0001; ns, not significant.

sec.p: Cytotoxicity assessed via CCK-8 assays in U87, patient-derived SHG141, and murine GL261 cells revealed significant, dose- and time-dependent cell killing by OVV-03. U87 cells exhibited cytotoxicity from 12 hpi (higher MOIs) through 48 hpi (all MOIs). SHG141 primary cells showed similarly potent dose-dependent cytotoxicity at 24 hpi and 48 hpi, but displayed delayed onset with no significant effect at 12 hpi compared to U87 cells. GL261 cells demonstrated comparable cytotoxicity kinetics, confirming broad efficacy (Figure 1D, Supplementary Figure 2B).

sec.title: OVV-03 induces apoptosis and suppresses clonogenic capacity in GBM cells in vitro
sec.p: To characterize the cytotoxic mechanism, we first quantified apoptosis induction using Annexin V/propidium iodide (PI) staining. OVV-03 infection triggered a substantial and significant increase in both early apoptotic (Annexin V⁺ PI⁻) and late apoptotic/necrotic (Annexin V⁺ PI⁺) cell populations in both the established U87 line and, critically, the patient-derived SHG141 primary GBM cells (Figure 2A–B). This robust induction of apoptosis across model systems underscores OVV-03's ability to overcome the intrinsic apoptotic resistance often observed in GBM. To gain spatial and functional insights, we performed immunofluorescence (IF) staining for key markers. OVV-03 treatment markedly suppressed cellular proliferation, evidenced by a significant reduction in Ki67-positive nuclei in both U87 and SHG141 cells. Simultaneously, OVV-03 potently activated the apoptotic cascade, demonstrated by a pronounced increase in cells staining positive for cleaved caspase-3 (C-casp3), the key effector caspase (Figure 2C–D). This dual action—inhibiting proliferation while actively executing cell death—highlights a multifaceted attack on GBM cell viability directly mediated by the virus. Using colony formation assays, we evaluated the impact of OVV-03 on long-term clonogenic survival. OVV-03 infection profoundly and significantly impaired the colony-forming ability of both U87 and SHG141 cells (Figure 2E–F). The near-complete ablation of colony formation at effective MOIs strongly suggests that OVV-03 effectively targets and eliminates the subpopulation of GBM cells responsible for tumor regrowth and recurrence, a significant challenge in clinical neuro-oncology. To elucidate the molecular pathways underlying OVV-03-induced apoptosis, we performed immunoblot analysis. OVV-03 treatment led to a significant upregulation of key apoptotic mediators: increased levels of cleaved caspase-3 (C-casp3), and cleaved poly ADP ribose polymerase (C-PARP), a well-established substrate of effector caspases and hallmark of committed apoptosis (Figure 2G). To substantiate the functional dependency on this pathway, we employed a caspase inhibition assay. Concurrently, pretreatment with the pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-FMK markedly attenuated the OVV-03-induced elevation of C-casp3 (Supplementary Figure 3A). This clear activation of the classical caspase-dependent apoptotic pathway provides a mechanistic foundation for the potent cytotoxic and pro-apoptotic effects observed. The induction of cleaved PARP is particularly significant, confirming the irreversible commitment to cell death.

caption.p: OVV-03 significantly kills GBM cells in vitro. (A) Annexin V and PI staining for detection of early and late apoptosis in U87 and SHG141 cells following OVV-03 infection. The x-axis represents Annexin V fluorescence intensity, and the y-axis represents PI fluorescence intensity. (B) Statistical analysis of apoptosis rate in (A), analyze the proportion of early apoptotic (Annexin V⁺ PI⁻) and late apoptotic (Annexin V⁺ PI⁺) cells (n = 3). (C) Immunofluorescence staining of U87 and SHG141 GBM cells was performed to assess the expression of Ki67 (green, a marker of proliferation) and cleaved-caspase 3 (C-casp3, red, a marker of apoptosis). Cell nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (blue). (D) Quantitative analysis of relative fluorescence intensity (MFI) in (C) (n = 3). (E) Analysis of colony formation experiment on the inhibition of clone formation ability by OVV-03. (F) Quantification of colony number from (E) (n = 3). (G) Western blot analysis of caspase 3 (Casp3), cleaved-caspase 3 (C-casp3), PARP, and cleaved-PARP (C-PARP) expression in U87 and SHG141 glioblastoma cells. β-tubulin was used as a loading control (n = 4). The statistical analysis was estimated by two-way or one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s correction. Data are presented as mean values ± SD. *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ***p < 0.001; ****p < 0.0001.

sec.title: OVV-03 exerts potent antitumor effects and remodels the glioma immune microenvironment in vivo
sec.p: OVV-03 controls intracranial tumor growth and extends survival. Longitudinal bioluminescence imaging revealed a steady and progressive increase in tumor-derived signals in control mice, culminating in uniform mortality. Intracranial administration of OVV-03, in stark contrast, induced rapid and sustained suppression of tumor growth, as evidenced by a significant decrease in bioluminescent signal intensity shortly after the first treatment. Quantitative analysis confirmed that the relative average radiance was significantly lower in the OVV-03 group compared to the control group. Critically, this therapeutic effect was completely abrogated in mice that received concomitant CD8+ T cell–depleting antibodies (OVV-03 + anti-CD8 group), where tumor progression kinetics mirrored those of the control group (Figure 3A–C). This result unequivocally demonstrates that the antitumor efficacy of OVV-03 is dependent on CD8+ T cells. Consequently, the potent tumor control observed in the OVV-03 group translated into a significant extension of median survival for tumor-bearing mice (Figure 3D). To dissect the immunological impact of OVV-03 within the brain TME, we performed flow cytometry on dissociated tumor tissue (Supplementary Figure 4). OVV-03 treatment significantly increased the total infiltration of CD45⁺ leukocytes and the frequency of CD45⁺ CD3⁺ T lymphocytes within the TME. Crucially, we observed a marked enrichment of CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) (Figure 3E-F). This shift towards a CTL-dominated infiltrate indicates that OVV-03 effectively counteracts the profoundly immunosuppressive GBM TME and promotes effector T-cell responses. OVV-03 elicits systemic antitumor immunity and the abscopal effect. To evaluate the induction of adaptive systemic immunity, we established bilateral subcutaneous GL261 glioma models in immunocompetent mice. Intratumoral injection of OVV-03 into the right flank tumor resulted in significant growth inhibition, with progressive tumor volume reduction over time (treated effect). Critically, robust suppression of tumor growth was also observed in the non-injected, contralateral left flank tumors (abscopal effect) (Figure 3G-H), subsequent immunofluorescence staining revealed a robust and significant increase in CD8+ T cell infiltration within the tumor microenvironment of the untreated left-sided tumors in the OVV-03-treated group, compared to the controls, and we found the presence of necrotic lesions in the untreated left tumor (Supplementary Figure 3B). This abscopal effect provides compelling evidence that OVV-03 treatment primes systemic tumor-specific T-cell responses capable of mediating antitumor immunity against distant, antigen-matched tumor sites, the recruitment of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells to distant, untreated tumor sites is the likely mechanism driving the observed abscopal effect, culminating in tumor cell death and necrosis. H&E staining revealed profound morphological alterations. Tumors from the OVV-03–treated group exhibited extensive geographic necrosis, complete disruption of cellular architecture, and loss of tissue integrity, control tumors retained compact and organized cellular structures (Figure 3I). This pattern of damage is consistent with the observed immune cell infiltration and systemic immune activation.

caption.p: OVV-03 exerts antitumor effects in vivo and remodels the tumor immune microenvironment. (A) Experimental timeline. An orthotopic immunocompetent mouse GBM model was established by intracranial implantation of 5 × 10⁵ GL261-Luc mouse glioma cells into C57BL/6 mice. On day 7 post-implantation, mice received an intratumoral injection of 1 × 109 PFU OVV-03 or vehicle. To evaluate the role of CD8+ T cells, one group received additional intraperitoneal injections of anti-mouse CD8 depleting antibody (0.1 mg) on days 7, 8, and 9. (B) Representative bioluminescent images showing GL261 tumor burden following the indicated treatments. (C) Quantification of relative average radiance from the control, OVV-03 and OVV-03 + anti-CD8 groups shown in (B). (D) Kaplan–Meier survival analysis of tumor-bearing mice (n = 5), with statistical significance assessed by log-rank test. (E) Flow cytometric analysis of T cell populations in the brains of treated mice. (F) Quantification of data presented in (E)(n = 6). (G-H) Subcutaneous immunocompetent GBM mouse models were generated by injecting 5 × 10⁵ GL261 cells into C57BL/6 mice, with tumors established either unilaterally (G) or bilaterally (H). On day 7 post-implantation, mice were intratumorally treated with 7 × 10⁹ PFU of OVV-03 or vehicle control every 3 days for a total of three doses at the right tumor site. On day 20, tumors were harvested for analysis (G, n = 4; H, n = 3). (I) H&E staining of subcutaneous tumors from control and OVV-03–treated mice in (G). Data are presented as mean ± SD. *p < 0.05; ***p < 0.001; ****p < 0.0001.

sec.title: OVV-03-mediated remodeling of the glioma immune microenvironment revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing
sec.p: To gain an unbiased, high-resolution view of how OVV-03 reshapes the complex glioblastoma immune landscape, we performed scRNA-seq on brain tissues from orthotopic GBM-bearing mice treated with OVV-03 or vehicle control. After rigorous quality control, we analyzed 17,861 high-quality single-cell transcriptomes. Unbiased clustering and UMAP visualization of the integrated dataset revealed well-defined cellular communities. Based on canonical marker gene expression profiles, we annotated ten major cell populations. malignant tumor cells, oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), endothelial cells (ECs), fibroblasts, B cells, T cells, neutrophils, macrophages (MPs), and microglia (Figure 4A). Marker gene expression across clusters confirmed the accuracy of cell type annotations, with each population exhibiting distinct and expected transcriptional signatures (Figure 4B).

caption.p: Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals the immunomodulatory effects of OVV-03 on the glioma microenvironment. (A) UMAP visualization showing clustering of single-cell transcriptomes from OVV-03 and control (Ctrl) treated tumors. (B) Heatmap of canonical marker gene expression across annotated cell populations. (C) Proportional distribution of cell types between Ctrl and OV groups. (D) Top 10 significantly downregulated KEGG pathways in cancer cells following OVV-03 treatment. (E) Top 10 downregulated KEGG pathways in CD8⁺ T cells in the OV group. (F) Heatmap of differentially expressed transcription factors between Ctrl and OV groups, highlighting OVV-03-induced changes in Fos, Junb, Stat1, and related regulators. (G) GO enrichment analysis of upregulated biological processes in CD8⁺ T cells, including T cell activation, cytotoxicity, and innate immune response.

sec.p: Comparative analysis revealed that OVV-03 treatment substantially reshaped the cellular architecture of the TME. Notably, OVV-03-treated tumors exhibited a marked increase in the relative abundance of T cells and macrophages, accompanied by a significant reduction in malignant cells and cells of the oligodendroglial lineage (including oligodendrocytes and OPCs) (Figure 4C). This shift from a tumor/stromal-dominant to an immune-enriched microenvironment suggests that OVV-03 not only reduces tumor burden through direct oncolysis but also promotes immune cell recruitment and/or expansion. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of malignant cell clusters revealed profound transcriptional reprogramming following OVV-03 treatment. Several pro-tumorigenic and immunosuppressive signaling pathways were significantly downregulated, most notably the TNF signaling pathway—implicated in inflammation-driven tumor progression—and the PD-L1/PD-1 immune checkpoint pathway, a central mechanism of tumor immune evasion (Figure 4D). Cell interaction analysis and single gene differential heatmap also demonstrate the impact of OVV-03 on tumor cell function (Supplementary Figure 5). These findings suggest that OVV-03 not only exerts cytolytic activity but also reprograms surviving tumor cells by downregulating key immunosuppressive mediators such as PD-L1. Further, transcription factor (TF) activity analysis in malignant cells demonstrated a significant downregulation of immediate-early response genes (e.g., Fos, Junb, Egr1), which are often associated with activation-induced dysfunction or cellular stress responses. In contrast, OVV-03 upregulated inflammatory and interferon-related TFs, including Stat1, indicative of enhanced responsiveness to interferon signaling—a key driver of antitumor immunity (Figure 4F). Complementary alterations were observed in CD8⁺ T cells. KEGG analysis of tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells from the OVV-03-treated group revealed a similar downregulation of the PD-1 signaling pathway (Figure 4E), suggesting a potential alleviation of T cell exhaustion. Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes in CD8⁺ T cells further validated this functional shift. OVV-03 treatment significantly upregulated biological processes directly linked to antitumor immunity, including T cell activation, cytotoxic effector functions (e.g., granzyme/perforin-mediated killing), and innate immune responses (Figure 4G). These transcriptional signatures collectively support a functional reprogramming of tumor-infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells toward a more activated and cytotoxic phenotype following OVV-03 therapy.

sec.title: TNFα reverses OVV-03–mediated PD-L1 downregulation via activation of the JNK–c-Fos/c-Jun signaling pathway
sec.p: To investigate the impact of OVV-03 on immune checkpoint modulation, we first assessed surface PD-L1 expression in GBM cell lines following OVV-03 infection. Flow cytometric analysis revealed a robust and consistent downregulation of PD-L1 on both U87 and SHG141 cells upon OVV-03 treatment, suggesting that OVV-03 may attenuate the immunosuppressive potential of tumor cells through modulation of PD-L1 expression (Figure 5A–B). To determine the functional consequences of this downregulation on T cell activity, we co-cultured CD3⁺ T cells with OVV-03–infected GBM cells and analyzed PD-1 expression on CD8⁺ T cells. The results demonstrated a significant decrease in PD-1 levels on CD8⁺ T cells following co-culture with OVV-03–treated tumor cells, indicating a potential reversal of T cell exhaustion and enhancement of T cell responsiveness (Figure 5C–D). To elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying OVV-03–mediated PD-L1 downregulation, we focused on the JNK–AP-1 signaling pathway, which is known to regulate PD-L1 transcription via the downstream effectors c-Fos and c-Jun. Western blot analysis demonstrated that OVV-03 treatment markedly suppressed the phosphorylation of JNK, c-Fos, and c-Jun, suggesting inhibition of this pathway as a mechanism for PD-L1 downregulation.In contrast, treatment with TNFα—a prototypical proinflammatory cytokine—led to robust activation of the JNK–c-Fos/c-Jun axis, as indicated by elevated phosphorylation of each component (Figure 5E, Supplementary Figure 6). Strikingly, when TNFα was applied to OVV-03–infected cells, the suppressed phosphorylation of JNK, c-Fos, and c-Jun was partially restored, indicating that inflammatory signaling can override the inhibitory effects of OVV-03 on this pathway. Consistent with the signaling data, flow cytometric analysis confirmed that TNFα treatment effectively reversed OVV-03–induced suppression of PD-L1 expression in both U87 and SHG141 cells (Figure 5F–G). These findings collectively demonstrate that OVV-03 downregulates PD-L1 expression through inhibition of the JNK–AP-1 signaling pathway, and that this effect can be counteracted by proinflammatory stimuli such as TNFα.

sec.title: OVV-03 sensitizes glioblastoma to CAR-T therapy through immune modulation and antigen upregulation
sec.p: To investigate whether OVV-03 could enhance the therapeutic efficacy of CAR-T therapy in glioblastoma, we employed an orthotopic GBM model in BALB/c nude mice. Tumor-bearing mice received intratumoral OVV-03 on day 7 post-implantation, followed by intracranial administration of CAR-T cells—either B7H3.CAR-T or HER2.CAR-T—on day 9 (Figure 6A). Combination treatment with OVV-03 and B7H3.CAR-T cells led to significantly greater tumor growth inhibition compared to either monotherapy (Figure 6B, D). Although OVV-03 did not significantly alter B7H3 antigen expression on tumor cells, its immunomodulatory effects—including PD-L1 downregulation and reshaping of the tumor microenvironment—likely contributed to enhanced CAR-T cell activity and tumor infiltration. Kaplan–Meier survival analysis revealed that mice treated with the combination therapy exhibited markedly prolonged survival relative to all other groups, highlighting the synergistic antitumor effect (Figure 6E). In the HER2.CAR-T cohort, OVV-03 exerted an additional benefit by upregulating HER2 expression on tumor cells, potentially improving CAR-T cell target recognition. This dual effect—antigen upregulation and immune environment remodeling—resulted in superior tumor suppression (Figure 6C, F) and significantly extended overall survival in the combination group compared to either treatment alone (Figure 6G). Collectively, these results indicate that OVV-03 enhances the efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy against GBM through both modulation of immune checkpoints and augmentation of tumor antigen expression, thereby improving CAR-T cell accessibility and cytotoxicity in the immunosuppressive GBM microenvironment.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we comprehensively characterized the antitumor efficacy and immunomodulatory properties of OVV-03, a novel oncolytic VSV-based therapy in GBM. Our findings demonstrate that OVV-03 not only exerts direct cytolytic effects on GBM cells but also potently remodels the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), thereby enhancing antitumor immunity and sensitization GBM to CAR-T cell therapies. Oncolytic viruses (OVs) possess the unique ability to selectively replicate within and destroy tumor cells while concurrently stimulating local and systemic immune responses, making them a promising platform for cancer immunotherapy. In the current study, OVV-03-engineered to express HER2 as a transgene-exhibited robust infectivity across multiple GBM cell lines and patient-derived cells, and induced apoptosis via activation of caspase-3 and PARP.24 These effects were validated using a range of assays, including Annexin V/PI staining, immunofluorescence for Ki67 and cleaved caspase-3, colony formation, and western blot analysis.25-27 Importantly, OVV-03 treatment also resulted in decreased proliferation and enhanced immunogenic cell death-both critical for initiating an effective antitumor immune response.28-30

In vivo, OVV-03 treatment significantly reduced tumor burden and prolonged survival in both orthotopic and subcutaneous GBM mouse models. Flow cytometry and scRNA-seq revealed substantial remodeling of the TIME, including increased infiltration of CD8⁺ CTLs,31,32 upregulation of immune activation pathways, and suppression of immunosuppressive signaling in both tumor and immune compartments.33,34 Notably, the downregulation of exhaustion-associated genes and transcriptional repressors in T cells suggests a reinvigoration of their effector functions. These findings highlight OVV-03's potential as a potent immunotherapeutic agent that not only kills tumor cells directly but also primes the host immune system for more effective tumor clearance. It is important to note that this study was conducted exclusively in female mice. Future studies incorporating male models are necessary to evaluate potential sex-dependent differences in the response to OVV-03.

Mechanistically, our results suggest that OVV-03 reduces PD-L1 expression on GBM cells by interfering with TNFα-induced activation of the JNK–c-Fos/c-Jun axis.35,36 This observation aligns with recent findings that the TME-derived cells and cytokines can modulate immune checkpoint expression, influencing T cell exhaustion and tumor evasion.37-40 Interestingly, exogenous TNFα administration reversed OVV-03–mediated PD-L1 suppression, further implicating the JNK signaling pathway in regulating immune checkpoints during OVV-based therapy. This modulation of PD-L1 suggests a dual mechanism of OVV-03 action—direct cytotoxicity and immune evasion blockade—offering an opportunity to enhance the efficacy of concurrent immunotherapies.41-44

Another critical dimension of our findings involves the strategic combination of OVV-03 with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells targeting either B7H3 or HER2. The enhanced efficacy observed in vivo, reflected by decreased tumor burden and prolonged survival, supports the hypothesis that OVV-03 can serve as an effective immune-sensitizing agent. By increasing the immunogenicity of GBM tumors and enhancing immune infiltration, OVV-03 may mitigate barriers that traditionally limit CAR-T cell access and activity in solid tumors.45,46 These data suggest that rational sequencing or co-administration of OV and CAR-T therapy may hold considerable translational value. It is important to note that the CAR-T cell combination studies presented here were conducted in immunodeficient mouse models. This approach was necessary to evaluate the synergy between OVV-03 and human HER2-specific CAR-T cells against human GBM tumors without confounding xenogeneic immune responses. While this setup robustly demonstrates direct tumoricidal synergy, it precludes analysis of the therapy's interaction with a fully intact immune system. Therefore, a crucial future direction will involve employing murine CAR-T cells targeting a surrogate antigen in immunocompetent, syngeneic GBM models. Such studies will be invaluable for dissecting the complex immunomodulatory crosstalk between OVV-03, CAR-T cells, and the native tumor microenvironment.

From a translational perspective, the choice of HER2 as the target antigen for OVV-03 and CAR-T therapy in glioblastoma presents both significant advantages and certain challenges. HER2 is expressed in more than 50% of glioblastoma specimens and remains relatively stable even in recurrent lesions, suggesting its potential as a durable target for immunotherapy. Moreover, HER2 expression is absent in the adult normal brain, which minimizes the risk of on-target, off-tumor toxicity—a critical safety consideration for intracranial therapies. These characteristics make HER2 an attractive and clinically feasible target for glioblastoma.

However, HER2 expression within glioblastoma is often heterogeneous, both spatially and temporally, which could limit uniform CAR-T recognition and facilitate immune escape. This intratumoral heterogeneity implies that a subset of tumor cells may remain HER2-negative and thus resistant to HER2-directed killing. In this context, the OVV-03 platform offers a potential solution by forcibly upregulating HER2 expression on infected tumor cells, thereby reducing antigenic variability and enhancing CAR-T cell accessibility. Nonetheless, the long-term stability of virally induced HER2 expression under immune pressure remains to be further validated in recurrent or post-treatment settings.

Further exploration into the kinetics and durability of OVV-03–induced immune responses is warranted. For instance, while acute responses following intratumoral OVV-03 administration were robust, it remains unclear whether memory T cell responses are established or if repeated dosing will be necessary for long-term tumor control.47 Investigating the phenotypic shifts within tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) over time and their functional capacity post-OVV-03 treatment could provide valuable insights into the development of durable antitumor immunity. Moreover, the spatial heterogeneity of GBM presents a unique challenge. The immunological and cellular landscape may vary significantly between the tumor core and periphery, potentially influencing the distribution and efficacy of OVV-03 and immune cells. Incorporating spatial transcriptomics could enhance our understanding of how OVV-03 reprograms the TIME across different tumor niches. Additionally, while our study focused on HER2 and B7H3 as CAR-T targets, other GBM-associated antigens such as IL13Rα2, EGFRvIII, and CD70 remain underexplored in the context of OV-enhanced immunotherapy.48-51 Finally, dose optimization, biodistribution studies, and toxicity profiling will be essential steps before clinical trials can be considered.52,53 Importantly, identifying biomarkers for response will help stratify patients who are most likely to benefit from OVV-03–based therapies.

Collectively, our findings position OVV-03 as a novel and promising agent within multimodal immunotherapeutic regimens for GBM. Its capacity to reprogram the TIME, converting immunologically “cold” tumors into “hot,” immunogenic lesions, addresses a fundamental barrier in current neuro-oncological management. This enhancement of tumor immunogenicity arises not only from direct oncolytic activity but also from potent immune activation and amplification, enabling significant synergy with adjunctive therapies such as CAR-T cells. These findings substantiate the paradigm of oncolytic viruses as potent immunotherapeutic agents with dual mechanisms of action: direct tumor cell lysis and systemic antitumor immune potentiation. Consequently, OVV-03 presents a promising strategy to overcome the limitations of existing GBM therapeutics.
